title: What changes each time round
prompt:
A `for` loop runs the same code once for every value in a vector. It reads
almost like English — *for each reading in sbp*:

```
for (reading in sbp) {
  ...
}
```

Each time round, the loop puts the next value of `sbp` into `reading`, then
runs the code between the curly brackets. The name `reading` is made up by
whoever wrote the loop; it could have been anything.

Click the name that holds a *different* value each time the loop goes
round.
hint:
After `for (`, one name is new — the loop makes it up. The other already
existed.

options.feedback:
Right. `reading` is a variable made up by the loop. The first time
round it holds 118, then 142, then 131, then 156 — one value from
`sbp` at a time.

One thing that surprises people: it doesn't disappear when the loop
ends. Afterwards, `reading` still exists, holding the last value, 156.
So if a later line uses `reading`, it quietly gets 156 — worth knowing
when you're reading code that reuses a name.

`sbp` is the whole set of values the loop walks through. It stays the
same the whole time; the loop takes one value from it on each pass.

This is the *body* — the code that runs each time round. It uses the
changing value, but it isn't the value itself.

title: What the loop prints
prompt:
What does this print?

```r
sbp <- c(118, 142, 131, 156)
for (reading in sbp) {
  print(reading - 10)
}
```
hint:
The body runs once for each reading, and `print()` shows something each
time it runs.

options.feedback:
Right — `print()` runs four separate times, and each run shows its own
line. Each line starts with `[1]` because each is a single value.

And look at the numbers: they're exactly what `sbp - 10` gave you in
module 5, in one line, with no loop. The loop took four steps to do
what R does to a whole vector at once.

That's what `sbp - 10` would print: one vector, shown on one line.
Here `print()` runs four separate times, and each run starts a new
line.

`print()` runs every time round, not only at the end, so every value
is shown.

title: A loop that seems to do nothing
prompt:
The same loop, without `print()`. What appears?

```r
sbp <- c(118, 142, 131, 156)
for (reading in sbp) {
  reading - 10
}
```
hint:
Outside a loop, R shows you each result automatically. Is that still true
inside one?

options.feedback:
Right, and it surprises nearly everyone. Inside a loop, R doesn't show
results unless something prints them. Each subtraction happens, and
each answer is thrown away.

Worth knowing when you're handed code: a loop that seems to do nothing
is often calculating something and discarding it, because nothing
stores or prints the result.

options.text: The four corrected readings, one per line
options.feedback:
That's what you'd get with `print()`. Without it, the results are
worked out and discarded — R only shows values automatically outside a
loop.

Not even the last one. Nothing inside the loop is shown unless it's
printed.

title: One line instead of a loop
prompt:
Generated code often builds a result with a loop like this:

```r
corrected <- c()
for (i in 1:length(sbp)) {
  corrected[i] <- sbp[i] - 10
}
```

`1:length(sbp)` makes the numbers `1 2 3 4`, so `i` counts through the
positions, and `sbp[i]` is the reading at each one. The loop fills
`corrected` one position at a time.

Write one line that gives the same `corrected`.
hint: You did this to a whole vector in module 5, with no loop at all.

solution.why:
Four lines of loop, one line of R. Arithmetic on a vector already
happens to every value, so the loop was doing by hand what R does on
its own.

That's why R code often doesn't need loops — and why, when generated
code has one, it's worth asking whether it could be a single line.
Shorter code has fewer places for a mistake to hide.

misconceptions.feedback:
That's the loop again. It works, but the point is that the whole thing
fits in one line — what does `sbp - 10` give you on its own?
That's `sbp` unchanged. Each reading still needs 10 taken off.

title: A counting loop in one line
prompt:
```r
high <- 0
for (reading in sbp) {
  if (reading > 140) high <- high + 1
}
high / length(sbp)
```

Read it piece by piece:

- `high <- 0` starts a count at zero.
- The loop goes through every reading, and adds one to the count each time
  a reading is over 140.
- The last line divides the count by the number of readings.

So the whole chunk works out the *fraction* of readings over 140, and gives
`0.5`. Which single line gives the same answer?
hint:
It's the *fraction* of readings over 140. In module 5, one function gave a
fraction of TRUEs rather than a count.

options.feedback:
Right. `sbp > 140` gives `FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE`, and the mean of TRUEs
and FALSEs is the fraction that are TRUE — here, 0.5. Five lines,
including an `if` inside a loop, become one.

That gives 2 — the count of high readings. The loop's last line divides
the count by the number of readings, which makes it a fraction.

That gives 4 — the number of answers, one per reading, whether TRUE or
FALSE.

That gives four TRUEs and FALSEs, one per reading. It's the question;
you still need to turn the answers into a single fraction.

title: Reading an if
hint: Work out `map < 65` first. Then follow the matching block.

options.feedback:
Right. `106 < 65` is FALSE, so R skips the first block and runs the one
after `else`. Only one of the two blocks ever runs.

One R quirk worth knowing: `else` has to come straight after the
closing `}`, on the same line. Put `else` on a line of its own and R
stops with an error, because it thinks the `if` has already
finished.

That block only runs when `map < 65` is TRUE. 106 isn't below 65, so R
skips it and runs the `else` block instead.

`if` picks exactly one block. The condition is either TRUE or FALSE,
and only the matching block runs.

title: An if given a whole column
prompt:
You were handed this to flag high readings:

```r
sbp <- c(118, 142, 131, 156)
if (sbp > 140) print("high")
```

What happens?
hint: How many TRUEs and FALSEs does `sbp > 140` give? How many can `if` take?

options.text: An error — `if` can only take one TRUE or FALSE
options.feedback:
Right: *the condition has length > 1*. `sbp > 140` gives four answers,
and `if` needs exactly one.

Worth knowing: before R 4.2, released in 2022, this ran anyway — `if`
quietly used the *first* answer and warned. Older examples online
still assume that, and so does code learned from them. When you want
an answer for every value, that's `ifelse()` from module 9:
`ifelse(sbp > 140, "high", "not high")`.

options.text: `"high"` is printed twice, once for each high reading
options.feedback:
That's what someone *means* by this, and it's a very natural reading.
But `if` isn't a loop: it takes a single TRUE or FALSE, and four
answers is an error.

options.text: It checks only the first reading, and prints nothing
options.feedback:
That's what older versions of R did, with a warning. Since R 4.2 it's
an error instead — `if` must get exactly one TRUE or FALSE.

title: A loop meets a missing value
hint:
On the second pass, `reading` is `NA`. What is `NA > 140`, and can `if`
act on that?

options.text: It stops with an error at the missing reading, and never checks 156
options.feedback:
Right: *missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed*. `NA > 140` is `NA`, and
`if` must have a definite TRUE or FALSE. The loop stops at the second
reading — so the 156, which really is high, is never looked at.

You've now seen three ways missing values behave. A filter invented a
patient (module 8), `t.test()` dropped one silently (module 10), and
here `if` stops loudly. This one is the good kind: you can't miss it.
`ifelse()` would give `NA` for that reading and carry on.

options.text: `"high"` once, for 156 — the missing one is skipped
options.feedback:
Skipping is what a reader might expect, but `if` can't skip. It needs
a TRUE or FALSE, and `NA > 140` is neither, so the loop stops there.

options.text: Nothing — none of them are printed
options.feedback:
Something does appear: an error, at the second reading. The loop never
gets as far as 156.

title: Why the double brackets?
prompt:
One more — nothing new, just things you already know turning up together.
This loop prints two pieces of the t-test result from module 10:

```r
for (name in c("p.value", "method")) {
  print(result[[name]])
}
```

Why does it use `result[[name]]` rather than `result$name`?
hint:
`$` takes whatever you type after it as the name. What would it look for
here?

options.text: `result$name` would look for a piece actually called "name"
options.feedback:
Right. There *is* a variable called `name` — on the first pass it holds
the text `"p.value"`. But `$` never looks inside a variable. It takes
whatever is typed after it as the name itself, so `result$name` means
*the piece of `result` called `name`*. There isn't one, so you get
`NULL`.

Double brackets work differently: R works out what's inside them
first. `result[[name]]` becomes `result[["p.value"]]`, which is the
p-value. That's why loops over the pieces of a *list* — often
`for (name in names(result))` — use `[[ ]]`.

options.text: They'd do exactly the same thing
options.feedback:
They would if the name were typed out, like `result$p.value`. But here
the name is held in the variable `name`, and `$` doesn't look inside
variables — it would search for a piece literally called `name`, and
find nothing.

Speed isn't the reason. `$` would take `name` as the piece's actual
name, and there's no piece called that.
